title: Another one writes the code
abstract:
Generative AI can now write code across the data science lifecycle and
produce plausible interpretations, challenging core assumptions about
what beginners should learn and how they should be assessed. This talk
examines the redesign of an introductory data science course at Duke
University in response to these shifts. Some changes were made because
of AI, including new in-class assessments; others were made thanks to
AI, such as integrating just-in-time feedback in the IDE. I will discuss
what changed, what failed, what improved, and how student
feedback—ranging from enthusiasm to skepticism—is shaping an evolving
approach to teaching data science in the age of generative AI.

title: What context do your AI agents actually need?
abstract:
Context window! AGENTS.md! Custom instructions! Agent skills! Max
tokens?? If you use AI agents in your data science work, you've probably
heard tips about these things and already use some of them. But does it
actually feel like your agents have the context they need about your
data, packages, and analysis? Or do you find yourself re-explaining your
data, spending more time editing agent output than doing the actual
task, or using up tokens faster than you'd like? Drawing on experience
building Positron's agent features, this talk covers how to manage
context: what kinds matter (from data to project structure), how to
include them (files you write in advance vs. fetching info on the fly),
and how to get results you don't have to rewrite.

title: AI Agents Deserve R
abstract:
R users have deep domain knowledge and finely-tuned workflows. You
should not have to abandon them to use AI. The R ecosystem already has
incredible building blocks: ellmer, shinychat, ragnar, and more. This
talk will cover some new entrants that such as deputy, dsprrr, and
shinymcp that grow the stack. Built on ellmer, deputy adds agentic
workflows. This includes agents that plan, use tools, and solve
multi-step tasks. dsprrr lets you program, not prompt, your LLM
pipelines. Compose modules and let data-driven optimization tune for
you. With coding agents making it easier than ever to port innovations
across languages, R's AI story has never been stronger. Stay in an
ecosystem you love and bring agents with you.

title: Public Policy in the Age of Demographic Uncertainty
abstract:
This talk showcases a dashboard that creates demographic projections for
regions across the United State of America to help drive impactful
policies aimed at creating better human outcomes. The tool leverages the
power of spatial statistics in R, Shiny, and the Apache Arrow ecosystem
to efficiently provide regionally specific insights. Forecasts and
projections are always challenging, however federal policy uncertainty
and an ongoing erosion to data quality are impeding our ability to plan
for the future. This talk discusses the headwinds to demographic data
creation and dissemination at the federal level and the implications
this could have for local jurisdictions to provide key services to their
communities.

title: MCP, or not MCP
abstract:
Model Context Protocol is a standard for defining tools that can be made
available to LLMs and AI applications. There’s a lot of noise out there
about what you should use to get the best results from AI, so in this
talk, I will provide some guidance on when you should use MCP, and when
you should reach for some other tool. I will describe cases where MCP is
the right tool for the job, and when other things, like skills or other
context files, are better. I will also devote attention to questions of
security and authentication, which are important for MCP. Some critics
of MCP have argued that they are risky, and I’ll discuss why. Then, I
will show how you can use MCP in a way that actually improves your
security and will delight IT admins.

title: Outgrowing Spreadsheets: Rebuilding Research Data Collection with Shiny and Posit Connect
abstract:
I’ll share how our nonprofit research team transformed a fragile,
spreadsheet-based data collection process into a sustainable system
using Shiny and Posit Connect. We publish a data set on 2,500 hospital
financial assistance programs and how they collect medical debt from
patients. Our team collected this data using Google Forms and sheets. It
technically worked, but it was fragile, slow, and completely dependent
on one person (me). When we finally got Posit Connect, we rebuilt the
system based on three principles: structured data entry, automated
validation, and recorded updates. This talk shares the before-and-after
architecture and practical lessons for teams ready to outgrow
spreadsheets and design sustainable workflows.

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Quarto
abstract:
Quarto markets itself as a publishing framework. But at its core, Quarto
is an abstraction layer separating \*content\* from \*format\* — a
distinction that turns out to be remarkably powerful in the era of AI
agents. When an LLM generates a document, content and structure emerge
together in a single probabilistic pass, but nothing in that output is
guaranteed. Quarto's code-at-render-time model solves this by letting
the LLM build the structure while allowing the content that must be
exact to be rendered deterministically from data files. The result is
reproducible and auditable output that stays correct as your content
changes, without needing to re-prompt models. This talk brings the
agent + Quarto workflow to life with concrete examples, from a simple
one-page PDF to a fully interactive multi-page dashboard integrating
JavaScript libraries, Shinylive, and React, showing how asking an LLM
for a qmd file instead of a finished document dramatically reduces token
overhead while producing more dynamic, trustworthy, and maintainable
output.

title: Say Yes to the Request - From Helping One to Empowering Many
abstract:
R adoption surged when we embraced one rule: say yes to every question
and turn each insight into something that lasts. To hit GSK’s 50%
R-by-2026 goal, STARburst—a small team of R experts—opened a helpdesk
focused on high-touch support. Each interaction followed a deliberate
user journey: we met people where they were, unblocked the immediate
task, then used that same moment to teach reusable habits for
open-source ways of working. In parallel, we logged every learning and
gap, turning recurring issues into R and Quarto assets: daily blogs and
FAQs first, then example libraries, hardened guidance, and improved R
packages. Attendees will see how bite-sized, one-to-one help compounds
into organization-wide R capability for the long haul.

title: SQL as a first-class language in your data science IDE
abstract:
Data scientists spend a lot of time and effort writing SQL, yet most
data science environments treat it as an afterthought or a separate
workflow, forcing you to switch tools, copy results between windows, and
lose context along the way. In this talk, learn how Positron brings SQL
into the same environment where you write Python and R code. We’ll walk
through connecting to databases, writing queries with intelligent code
completion, executing SQL in a dedicated console, and exploring results
in the Data Explorer. You’ll see how keeping SQL alongside your other
data science work reduces friction and errors. This talk is for data
scientists and analysts who regularly query databases and want to stop
context-switching between tools.

title: A Grammar of Graphics for SQL
abstract:
SQL has been with us for many years, but despite its age it is still a
cornerstone of data-analysis everywhere. The quick success of DuckDB
shows this more than ever. However, SQL is often used as the first step
to extract data, delegating any search for insight to a different
programming language or environment. I would like to present ggsql, an
extension of SQL that provides a grammar of graphics on top of SQL and
allows you to create visualisations directly within your query. ggsql is
a modular tool, build to interface directly with your data source and
optimised for use by an LLM based data analysis workflow due to its lack
of runtime.

title: One Report, Many Audiences: Role‑Based Views in Posit Connect
abstract:
Harvard University’s decentralized structure creates diverse data needs
across its many schools. Our central institutional research office uses
Posit Connect to share data and reports, but not every person should see
the same content. To address this, we published a Shiny app on Posit
Connect that detects the logged‑in user and dynamically tailors what
they see. This means that a single report can securely serve many
audiences. This talk will walk through how the pieces fit together and
offer a model for organizations seeking scalable, user‑aware reporting.

title: Quarto Wiki Chatbot
abstract:
After a year of compiling onboarding, technical, and other documentation
into a centralized Quarto Wiki, NASA’s People Analytics team still
struggled to quickly search for needed information. We developed an
integrated chatbot, which surfaces and cites relevant content to answer
user questions - processing QMD files into a vector database, developing
a Python RAG pipeline, and embedding an R Shiny chat window into the
Quarto site’s interface. To reduce latency and long-term LLM costs,
DuckDB caches and scores prior query-response pairs for selective reuse.
The system can be deployed on Posit Connect or run locally, illustrating
a reproducible workflow for interactive, AI-assisted documentation.
Presented by: Aliza Samad and Sofia Lendahl.

title: Template → Package → App: Meeting Users Where They're At
abstract:
We built a reporting workflow to help farmers turn complex soil health
data into useful management decisions. What started as a Quarto template
for one specific project became the {soils} R package for other coders,
and eventually Dirt Data Reports, a Shiny app for people who don't code.
This talk is about what we learned while lowering barriers at each step.
Building for the user means choosing the right level of flexibility,
abstraction, and complexity for the people you're trying to reach. The
goal isn't to create one perfect tool; it's to meet users where they're
at.

title: SQL Without Writing SQL: dbplyr for Serious Shiny Apps
abstract:
You don't need to be an SQL expert or a DBA to build high-performance
Shiny apps on large datasets. With dbplyr, you can write familiar dplyr
code while it translates your pipelines into optimized SQL behind the
scenes. In this talk we will explore how integrating Shiny with Postgres
SQL and how the dplyr you write today can translate to better performing
applications. We will cover practical patterns to keep computation in
the database to create production-ready apps without leaving R.

title: Keynote Session: How to Be Clear When You Can’t Be Certain
abstract:
Sometimes, data visualization is about using charts to illustrate a key
point or conclusion gleaned from analyzing the data. But what if you’re
not sure what the conclusion is? Presenting examples from news reporting
on the topics of elections, polling and economics, I will talk about how
I have grappled with uncertainty and how to communicate it to the
public.

title: For the community, by the community: The 10-year journey of R Weekly powered by open-source
abstract:
For a decade, R Weekly has highlighted the innovations, creativity, and
novel resources tailored to the R language across data science. Built
and sustained by a small, volunteer curator team, the project
demonstrates how open-source values—transparency, collaboration, and
shared ownership—can power a lasting community initiative. This talk
explores how R Weekly evolved, the workflows and infrastructure that
keep it running, and the lessons learned from ten years of amplifying
innovation. This talk will demonstrate how community-driven curation can
strengthen ecosystems and inspire sustainable open-source contributions.

title: Interdependent Filters in Shiny Made Simple
abstract:
Developing interdependent filters in Shiny has always been tedious,
requiring developers to rewrite custom ui and server logic for each new
app. The new R package shinyfilters exists to eliminate this
boilerplate. shinyfilters lets anyone create interdependent filters
directly from data.frames. I am excited to show attendees how
shinyfilters uses S7 to simplify interdependent filter logic, how to
replace repetitive ui and server code with simple function calls, and
how to extend shinyfilters for their own use cases.

title: Beyond Bootstrap: Building Custom Shiny UI Packages with AI
abstract:
Shiny developers have long been limited to Bootstrap and a handful of
pre-built UI frameworks. But what if you could use Material UI, Ant
Design, or any modern react.js web framework you love?\
\
This talk demonstrates how AI can generate production-ready R packages
that wrap your favorite UI frameworks for Shiny. We'll walk through
using AI to translate JavaScript components into R bindings, handle
dependencies, and create idiomatic interfaces—no JavaScript expertise
required.\
\
You'll see live examples, learn effective prompting patterns, and
discover how to maintain AI-generated packages. Whether you want
Material Design or Web Components, AI makes it possible to bring any UI
framework into your Shiny apps.

title: Quarto Notebooks and Literate Programming in Positron
abstract:
Quarto Notebooks, a new Positron feature, give you access to Jupyter's
literate programming features without losing any of the benefits of
working with plain text for editing, versioning, and collaborating. They
are a natural evolution of the R Markdown Notebooks feature in RStudio
into the modern, multi-lingual environment of Quarto and Positron. In
this talk, I'll introduce this new way of working, and describe both its
similarities and differences to its predecessor in RStudio. Finally,
we'll spend some time comparing the different tools for literate
programming in Positron, their tradeoffs, and how to choose the right
one.

title: ADBC: A Faster Foundation for Database Connectivity in R, Python, and Beyond
abstract:
dplyr was a revolution for R, and dbplyr was a smaller but important
revolution for those of us who wanted to use databases without leaving
behind the powerful and familiar syntax of dplyr. The arrow R package
was another revolution of its own, letting us work with
larger-than-memory data while still using dplyr syntax. Apache Arrow,
the larger project of which the arrow R package is a part, also has a
standard for database access: ADBC. In this talk, I’ll introduce ADBC,
which works with R, Python, and other languages and is coming to dbplyr.
I’ll give an intro to Arrow and ADBC, and show how to use a new command
line tool, dbc, along with dbplyr, for fast, larger-than-memory database
access that works seamlessly across R and Python.

title: Yes And...AI in Your IDE
abstract:
Large language models are now embedded in our IDEs, shaping how we code.
Research suggests assistants don’t respond “neutrally”: how you ask and
even cues about who is asking can shift what the model says. In this
session, we’ll explore what that looks like with Posit’s AI tools that
draw on IDE context. We’ll run simple “paired prompts”: same problem,
different asker then compare their agreement, and whether the assistant
challenges assumptions or amplifies them. This talk is about using LLMs
while involving the user, and bringing in the decision-making before the
result. Bring curiosity, your critical thinking, and a healthy suspicion
of anything that agrees with you a little too easily.

title: Shiny design: Where humans and AI disagree
abstract:
AI can generate Shiny dashboards, grade visual quality from screenshots,
and tweak their own code. But do they actually like the same designs
people do? We pitted automated visual scores against blind human
rankings across dashboards built by different models, frameworks, and
prompts. I'll share where machine taste matches human judgment, where it
completely falls off, and what these gaps tell us about visual design.
Finally, we'll look at how human input can spot the flaws in automated
scoring so we can build far better AI evaluators.

title: From Tribal Knowledge to Trusted AI in Pharma
abstract:
Everyone wants to know how to build useful AI. We learned that the
hardest part wasn’t the technical implementation at all.

We expected embeddings, entity extraction, retrieval pipelines, and
plenty of AI plumbing. Instead, the work that mattered most was sitting
with pharmaceutical sales reps, uncovering tribal knowledge, resolving
conflicting definitions, and turning years of business logic from Shiny
apps on Posit Connect into governed logic in Snowflake.

This talk shows what changed once we built around how people actually
work. We’ll share how user feedback shaped the language, rules, UX, and
priorities of the system, and how that human context made the AI more
trustworthy, explainable, and useful in the field.

title: Influence with Quarto: Designing Reports That Drive Decisions
abstract:
Most people using Quarto already know how to render documents. This talk
focuses on what comes next: elevating Quarto reports through design,
layout, and narrative. Using a realistic example report, I’ll show how
styling, visual hierarchy, and thoughtful structure can transform a
technically correct analysis into a compelling story for
decision-makers. The goal isn’t more code, but better communication:
using the right data storytelling, CSS, and ggplot to create reports
that feel intentional, polished, and impactful. Attendees will leave
with concrete ideas to push their own Quarto reports beyond defaults.

title: Repotting and propagating my Shiny houseplant
abstract:
My Shiny app started out as a single seed: one app.R. Its quick growth
became restricted by its tiny pot as features tangled together. So, I
repotted my app.R file into 11 modules to organize my UI and server
logic. My Shiny plant kept growing, but with better structure. To share
my thriving plant with friends and clients, I learned how to propagate
cuttings to create new, similar apps by turning it into a package. This
let me reuse the core code across apps, while making pieces
customizable. To update calculations or aesthetics, I now update the
package code once, rather than editing 10 different apps. This talk will
walk through the app growth cycle, what triggers each step, and how to
repot and propagate without killing your Shiny plant.

title: Hello, robot: Introducing humans to LLM’s
abstract:
You know that AI can be transformative when used correctly, but how do
you train your team – or organization – to be effective AI users? Last
year we tackled this problem through a course that built foundational
LLM skills for staff at Posit. By focusing on learner curiosity,
personal experience and experimentation, we helped teams across the
organization develop relevant skills with AI tools. In this talk, I'll
share some details of our approach, lessons we learned, and ideas on how
to scale this type of learning within an organization; I will also debut
a publicly-accessible version of the course.

title: High Quality R/Shiny Apps at Scale: Lessons from DaVinci’s Modular Framework
abstract:
Scaling R/Shiny apps is hard: code gets duplicated, UX becomes
inconsistent, and validation is expensive. With DaVinci, a Shiny
framework for exploring clinical trial data, we address these issues
through a modular approach. DaVinci provides reusable, qualified modules
that follow shared standards for structure, interfaces, testing, and
performance. This talk shows why modularity works at scale, how it
speeds up delivery and improves quality, and how module developers, app
creators, and app users work together to build robust apps. Attendees
will learn practical patterns to improve consistency, maintainability,
and validation effort – applicable to any team building many Shiny apps,
not only in pharma.

title: From chats to workflows to “agents”: Demystifying LLM jargon by example
abstract:
If the phrase "agentic AI" has ever made you scratch your head (or roll
your eyes), this talk is for you. The AI field is awash in jargon that
sounds precise but isn't—and when every technology is branded as an
"agent" or "agentic," it’s pretty hard to know what anyone is talking
about. So, let's fix that. In this gentle, no-experience-required
introduction to LLM systems, I'll demystify the jargon by building up
from first principles. Using a single running example—turning messy
clinical notes into a structured summary—we'll walk through four levels
of LLM system design: chats, workflows, agents, and multi-agent systems.
You'll leave with a better understanding of agentic design patterns and
how to try them out for yourself.

title: Better Python Notebooks with Marimo
abstract:
Interactive notebooks are foundational to applied data science, but
notebook-based workflows can be plagued by out-of-order execution,
difficult storage formats, and unwanted input-output mixing. Marimo is a
modern, batteries-included Python notebook system that tackles these
problems head-on, and this talk will discuss how some of Marimo’s core
features make notebook workflows safer and more productive. We’ll
highlight features that make notebooks both safer to use and fit more
naturally into data science workflow, from Marimo’s reactive execution
model to its script-based format and native support for sandboxed
environments.

title: The modern tool builder: CLIs, agents, and PEP 723
abstract:
Being able to write R or Python scripts is an incredibly useful skill,
allowing you to automate nearly any task imaginable. However, with a bit
of extra effort, those brittle scripts can be transformed into robust,
reusable tools. In particular, tools that you can run from the command
line or that can be run by coding agents. Future-you will thank you for
making the extra effort.

In this talk, we will explore why you should graduate from writing
scripts to building tools, particularly command-line interfaces (CLIs).

CLIs have been around for over 50 years. Thanks to the rise of coding
agents, being able to understand and use the command line is now more
important than ever. I'd say there are three reasons for this. First,
coding agents rely on CLI tools such as find, grep, and git (and maybe
yours!). Second, some coding agents, such as Claude Code, are themselves
CLI tools that you can incorporate into your scripts. Third, agents are
actually really good at helping you to build your own tools, so if you
use them there's really no excuse anymore.

title: Positron and the Three Bears: Teaching Python with Positron
abstract:
For polyglot data science, RStudio is too specific, VS Code is too
general, but Positron is just right. However, it’s not without friction.
With two years of experience teaching Python with Positron, I’ll discuss
how Positron fits in the data stack and how it helps address the “three
bears” of teaching Python: 1. Installing Python and managing virtual
environments 2. Creating GitHub-friendly notebook workflows 3. Accessing
scalable compute resources I hope my experience with Positron can help
other attendees in their professional and personal efforts as
instructors and mentors.

title: Delivering Automations at Scale: {rtemplate} for High‑Throughput Biomarker Analytics
abstract:
Supporting hundreds of biomarker focused clinical and exploratory
studies requires fast, standardized, and reproducible early stage
analyses in the biopharma industry. After exploring approaches and needs
of analysts and scientists, our team converged on {rtemplate} - an R
based automation framework that easily delivers structured data via
{arrow}, an orchestrated analysis pipeline via {targets}, consistent
figure standards via {ggplot2}, and Quarto powered {shiny} viewers. With
by AI assisted feature development, {rtemplate} enables teams to meet
tight timelines while shifting analyst time toward the deep, high impact
scientific work that matches the reality of clinical and exploratory
biomarker workloads. Developed in collaboration with Peter Ehmann,
previously with Regeneron, now with Merck & Co., Inc.

title: Making the Impossible Possible: A Software-First Stack for Resource-Constrained Research
abstract:
At Drexel's Urban Health Collaborative, we study how climate change
affects health across US and Latin American cities — complex work run by
a small team with no enterprise budget. I'll share how Posit's
code-first products took us from ad hoc data management to a
software-first organization. Starting from RStudio, Quarto turned
pipelines into reproducible notebooks and Positron opened the door to
Python tools like dbt-DuckDB. That let us adopt analytics engineering,
GitHub-driven development, and Notion for non-technical collaboration —
shipping model-ready data fast. This code-first stack is ready for
what's next: agentic AI. Attendees leave with a playbook for a
lightweight data stack resource-constrained teams can adopt
incrementally.

title: From Programming Alone to Programming and Prompting: Teaching Bilingual AI-Enabled Data Science with Positron and Quarto
abstract:
Most courses teach R or Python. I teach both—in the same Quarto
documents, using Positron. Students start with parallel tracks
(bag-of-words, NLP in both languages), then shift mid-semester to
integrated workflows: R for preprocessing, Python for transformers. But
I've moved beyond programming alone. Prompt engineering starts week two.
GitHub Copilot and Positron Assistant are available from day one, with
prompting exercises in every lab. These bilingual, AI-augmented skills
are essential. One surprise: students with no prior programming
experience end up more bilingual than those who arrive knowing one
language. No home base to retreat to. I'll share what's working, what's
not, and how Positron and Quarto make this practical.

title: Designing Reproducible Learning Ecosystems with R and Quarto
abstract:
Reproducibility in data science is often taught as a final requirement
rather than as a workflow that evolves over time. This talk presents a
reproducible learning ecosystem built with R and Quarto that moves
learners from one-off assignments to durable, public work—and ultimately
into contributors. Learners iteratively refactor their analyses into
portfolio books, contribute to a shared research volume built on real
civic data, and engage with open tooling that lowers barriers to
authentic analysis. The session focuses on design decisions, lessons
learned, and practical patterns for teaching reproducibility through
iteration, ownership, and real-world data.

title: Bridging the Gap: Custom Catalogs to Connect End Users with Data Products
abstract:
For data scientists today, creating stellar apps and reports is not
enough without proper dissemination to the end users. Our team has
created dozens of Shiny apps and Quarto reports which can be useful to
the wider organization. Now, to bridge the gap between our users and
data products, we have developed an interactive catalog with Quarto
Dashboard, the connectapi R package, and a content tags hierarchy on
Connect. We aim to help end-users explore our offerings and quickly find
the tools they can most benefit from. My talk will demonstrate how any
data analytics team can easily build their own custom catalog to better
communicate with their end users.

title: The Tableau Plateau: From Dashboards to AI-Ready Data Products
abstract:
At Suffolk, we hit a “Tableau plateau.” Our team had split into two
tribes: point-and-click dashboard builders and code-first data
scientists. BI tools felt faster - but capped our technical ceiling. By
standardizing on Shiny, using Git-backed deployment for Posit Connect,
and leveraging AI coding agents like Positron Assistant, we flipped the
equation. With Shiny modules and brand.yml providing guardrails for
developers and agents, we standardized structure, styling, and patterns.
Code not only surpassed point-and-click tools in speed - it produced
extensible products built for ML and AI integration. This shift unified
our team and transformed dashboards from reporting artifacts into
AI-ready data products.

title: Posit Pro Product Updates
abstract:
Join this special session to hear the latest product updates from Posit,
including Posit Workbench, Connect, Package Manager, the Posit Team
Native App for Snowflake, Connect Cloud, and Posit AI. This session will
have 5 talks!

- **Trust in the Cloud: Secure Deployments and Effortless AI Access \|
  Alex Chisholm \| Posit**\
  Data science professionals and their teams face growing governance
  questions. What's been deployed, where the data lives, and which
  models have seen it. At the same time, they - and the system admins
  watching over it all - want the ease and speed that cloud deployments
  promise. Too often, speed and governance get treated as opposing
  goals, but they don't have to be.\
  In this talk, we'll show how Connect Cloud and a Posit AI subscription
  are built to deliver both. Connect Cloud, now through its first SOC 2
  Type 1 audit, lets you publish from RStudio, Positron, GitHub, or the
  command line, with scheduling and custom domains that empower everyone
  without the infrastructure overhead. A Posit AI subscription powers
  Posit Assistant and Next Edit Suggestions with a curated set of
  validated models, plus Zero Data Retention coverage and full control
  over your data so that speed and trust don't have to be a tradeoff.\
  Not every organization can operate entirely in the cloud for every use
  case. But for the teams who can, we want to offer the easiest, safest
  choice possible.
- **Enterprise Data Science, Minus the Overhead: Posit Team Native App
  on Snowflake \| Chetan Thapar \| Posit**\
  If you're a data scientist at an enterprise running Posit's pro
  products, the odds are you aren't on a recent version. The products
  keep improving; the environment you actually work in updates once a
  year, if that. If you're the platform admin, you know why. Every
  upgrade is a project: infrastructure, coordination, downtime, security
  review. And standing the platform up in the first place was a bigger
  project still - infra, software, role provisioning - before a single
  data scientist ran their first analysis. The Posit Team Native App
  runs Workbench, Connect, and Package Manager natively inside your own
  Snowflake account. Access is instant: install from the Marketplace,
  start a self-service trial, and be working in minutes. Ops headaches
  go away: it's a fully managed service, upgrades arrive automatically
  and typically monthly, roles are inherited from Snowflake rather than
  provisioned twice, and your data never leaves your perimeter. And
  productivity compounds: your data scientists get the latest releases
  without the platform overhead; all three are wired to work together
  out of the box; and Posit Assistant runs on Cortex-hosted LLMs with
  semantic model awareness, no configuration required. Instant access,
  no ops headache, accelerated productivity. This session is what we've
  delivered against each of these recently, where we still have work to
  do, and what's coming next, including an early look at R MLOps on
  Snowflake.
- **Beyond Packages: Governing the AI Toolchain with Posit Package
  Manager \| Joe Roberts \| Posit**\
  Posit Package Manager started as a way to govern R and Python packages
  — mirroring, curating, and controlling what makes it into your
  environments. That job hasn't gone away, but it's no longer the whole
  story.\
  As AI agents become part of everyday data science work, teams need the
  same governance discipline applied to a new set of artifacts: VS Code
  extensions, AI plugins, and the growing ecosystem of tools that agents
  use to get work done. In this talk, we'll look at how Package Manager
  is expanding to meet that need.\
  We'll start with a practical overview of AI plugins — what they are,
  what capabilities they expose, and why curating them matters as much
  as curating packages. From there, we'll show how PPM acts as a private
  marketplace for these plugins, and how Posit Assistant and other AI
  agents can connect to that marketplace directly. Finally, we'll get
  hands-on with PPM's MCP server, showing how it makes agent-to-PPM
  integration straightforward, and how AI plugins themselves can define
  MCP servers hosted on Posit Connect and elsewhere — turning your
  governed package repository into a governed tool repository.\
  You'll leave with a clear picture of where package management is
  headed as AI agents join the data science workflow, and concrete ideas
  for how to keep that expansion safe, curated, and useful.
- **Building Posit Connect for Two Very Different AI Organizations \|
  Kelly O’Briant & Matt Leary \| Posit**\
  As product managers of Posit Connect, we get to talk to a lot of
  different kinds of organizations about how they’re using AI. \
  Some have AI everywhere. Every department has its own assistants.
  There are dozens of chat applications, hundreds of prototypes, and new
  tools appearing faster than anyone can keep track of. Success has
  created a lot of questions: Who owns these applications? Which models
  are they using? What data can they access? Who is monitoring them?\
  Others are still struggling to get started. People want to build
  AI-powered tools, but security, IT, and legal can't agree on how to
  move forward. The most ambitious employees find consumer AI tools on
  their own, while the most cautious wait for solutions or decisions
  that may never arrive. \
  These organizations look completely different. What they need,
  however, is remarkably similar.\
  In this talk, I'll show how we're building Posit Connect to support
  both of these organizations. The details differ, but the destination
  is the same: a platform where anyone can publish useful AI-powered
  work, regardless of language or framework, while giving administrators
  the visibility and control they need to make AI sustainable across the
  organization.
- **AI Governance: Bringing Posit Assistant to the enterprise \| Thomas
  Mock \| Posit**\
  As data science teams rapidly integrate AI, the challenge lies not
  merely in achieving correct analysis, but in demonstrating that
  results are trustworthy and compliant. While tools like Posit
  Assistant bring powerful, code-first, and session-aware data science
  assistance to RStudio and Positron, many organizations struggle with
  implementation by retrofitting governance as a separate,
  friction-heavy layer.\
  This presentation explores a shift toward architectural governance,
  integrating oversight directly into the infrastructure rather than
  applying it as an external control. We will demonstrate a model built
  on four core pillars: code-first design, human-in-the-loop workflows,
  session-aware data privacy, and governed environments. By leveraging
  unified infrastructure, we can align the needs of data scientists with
  the requirements of IT, compliance, and security teams. Attendees will
  learn how to move governance from an administrative burden to a
  seamless, inherent feature of the data science lifecycle.

title: Everything you wanted to know about agents* (*but were afraid to ask)
abstract:
Agents, agents, agents. The practice of software development has been
transformed by AI coding agents like Claude Code. The practice data
science is also being changed by AI coding agents, but not quite in the
same way. Data science uses many of the same tools and techniques as
pure software development, but at its heart there is a fundamental
difference: with software development, the goal is to build something,
but with data analysis, the goal is to learn something. With that in
mind, I’ll talk about: - What is an agent? - How do they work? - What
are they good at, and what are they bad at? - How is software
development different from data science? - How can you maximize your
trust in agent’s work?

title: Great Docs: Beautiful Documentation Sites for Python Packages
abstract:
Documentation is one of the most impactful things you can do for your
Python package (and one of the most tedious to set up). Between manually
cataloging your API, wrestling with configuration, and keeping
everything in sync as your code evolves, many projects ship with
incomplete docs (or none). Great Docs eliminates this friction. A single
command auto-discovers your package's public API and generates a
complete, professionally styled documentation site. It also
auto-generates llms.txt files, creates license and citation pages, and
gives you a polished landing page, organized API reference, and User
Guide section. In this talk, I'll introduce Great Docs, walk through its
workflow, and demo sites I've built for several Python projects.

title: Less to decide, more to reuse: the block in blockr
abstract:
We present blockr, a framework for interactively building data
workflows, developed in collaboration with Bristol-Myers Squibb.
Implemented as a modular set of R packages, blockr suits applications
from interactive dashboards to static reports. The break-down into
well-defined steps, along with AI assistance, provides a natural,
no-code interface to complex problems. A block is a deliberately
restricted unit of computation, and this is what lets the same blocks be
reused across very different applications. We show what it takes to
write a block. We then look at a production app built almost entirely
from general-purpose blocks, with domain-specific ones only where the
problem demands them, and an AI assistant to assemble them.

title: Debugging Is a Nightmare: Meaningful Metaphors for Data Science Education
abstract:
Metaphor and analogy are often treated as rhetorical flourishes, but
they play a real role in how we learn technical concepts. In data
science education, metaphors help make invisible processes visible and
support transfer from familiar experience into abstract reasoning. This
talk treats “debugging is a nightmare” as more than a phrase, using it
to guide concrete practices like “dream journaling” (minimal
reproducible examples), “lucid dreaming” (stepping through code), and
“magic apples” (capturing state). It then steps back to reflect on how
such frames shape learners’ reasoning, where they help, where they break
down, and what educators should be deliberate about in choosing
appropriate metaphors.

title: Finding Common Language between Data Scientists and Non Data Scientists
abstract:
Data scientists need to communicate effectively with stakeholders who do
not have a programming background but do have detailed technical
knowledge in an area where the data scientist is not an expert. Finding
the right shared language helps minimize wasted work, especially early
in a project. For example: cooking recipes can serve as an analogous
data set understood by synthesis chemists and data scientists working on
chemical reaction data. Use of a common language reduces the amount of
brainpower spent interpreting terminology and allows everyone to focus
on design goals – data visualizations, search interfaces, data sources,
etc. This talk will provide advice for finding a shared language topic
and examples of how they can be used.

title: SELECT instance FROM cloud WHERE workload = ? ORDER BY cost_efficiency
abstract:
Selecting the right cloud instance for DS/ML/AI workloads is still
mostly guesswork. Pricing and hardware specs exist, but fragmented
across providers and hard to compare, especially when real workload
performance matters. We introduce Spare Cores Navigator, an open dataset
covering thousands of cloud instance types across vendors with
standardized performance and cost-efficiency metrics. We show how
instance choice becomes a simple data task in R or Python: filter by
workload, hardware, compliance, or budget, then rank candidates by
price-performance to identify the most efficient option for your
workload.

title: Finding Care Fast: An R Shiny App for Infectious Disease Exposure Response
abstract:
Local public health agencies must rapidly coordinate testing and
vaccination for people who have been exposed to infectious diseases. At
DeKalb Public Health, epidemiologists previously relied on manual Google
Maps searches to identify the closest of four health centers for each
patient. To address this complicated and time-consuming process, I
developed an R Shiny app that ranks centers by driving distance using
ZIP code centroids to preserve privacy. I utilized the openrouteserve
API to calculate the distances and used the leaflet package to create
interactive maps. The app supports single and batch address workflows,
reduces coordination time, and demonstrates how open-source tools can
have real-world impact in public health.

title: Keynote Sessions: Correct, reproducible, and transparent data agents (Sara & Simon), Building the Future of Data Science and AI with Posit and AWS (Jagjit Dhaliwal)
abstract:
9 - 9:55am \| How do we build competent data analysis agents? Data
analysis requires a willingness to pause, question conclusions, dig into
subtleties, and sit with uncertainty. Frontier LLMs, however, are
optimized to push tasks toward completion rather than refraining from
answering unanswerable questions. Drawing on our experience building
data analysis agents, we'll share evaluations that expose where
LLM-driven analysis goes wrong and design patterns that keep analyses
correct, transparent, and reproducible.

title: Positron for Everyone: Organization-Wide Posit Tooling on Amazon SageMaker
abstract:
Unlock the full potential of your analytics team by deploying Positron
as a managed, organization-wide environment within Amazon SageMaker
Studio. This joint session with Posit and AWS explores how to provide
analysts with a browser-based, scalable IDE equipped with R, Python, and
Quarto, all while maintaining seamless AWS integration. We will detail
the analyst experience, including built-in AI assistance via
Bedrock-powered Posit Assistant, and provide technical insights for
platform teams on managing deployments, licensing, and security at
scale. Eliminate local environment friction and empower your
organization with a unified, cloud-native workspace.

title: Lunch & Learn: Bridging R, Python, and Snowflake: AI-Assisted Workflows and Native MLOps with Positron
abstract:
Join us for an interactive Lunch & Learn session demonstrating how Posit
tools integrate with Snowflake’s data and AI capabilities to streamline
full-lifecycle data science.

**Part 1: AI-Assisted Development with Positron, Snowflake Skills, and
Cortex LLMs.** Experience the next generation of data science workflows
inside Positron, Posit's polyglot IDE. We will demonstrate how Posit
Assistant combines with custom Snowflake skills and Cortex LLMs to help
you query data, write optimized code, and leverage secure,
enterprise-grade AI models, all without leaving your development
environment.

**Part 2: End-to-End MLOps with snowflake-r and Snowflake's Model
Registry.** Take models from prototype to production using native R and
Python tooling. We will walk through an end-to-end MLOps workflow
leveraging the open-source snowflake-r community packages. Learn how to
engineer features, train models, register versioned artifacts, and
deploy them for scalable, in-database scoring, bringing your code
directly to the data.

**Part 3: Reporting: What Posit Connect can do for you.** After creating
a model, vibecode a Shiny frontend and deploy it to Connect with one
click!

Whether you are looking to accelerate daily coding with integrated LLM
assistants or establish robust, scalable MLOps pipelines across R and
Python, this session offers practical patterns you can immediately apply
to your team's stack.

**Key Takeaways for Attendees**

- How to leverage **Posit Assistant** in Positron with tailored
  **Snowflake skills** and **Cortex LLMs**.
- How to use **snowflake-r packages** to interact smoothly with
  Snowflake data pipelines.
- Best practices for managing features and registering models with
  **Posit and Snowflake**

title: The Shiny AI Stack: shinychat, querychat, and the LLM Plumbing Beneath
abstract:
LLM-powered chat is becoming a core pattern in modern Shiny apps, but
building a good chat experience (i.e., streaming, history, file
attachments, editing, cancellation, etc) — is harder than it looks. In
this talk, we'll tour the Shiny AI stack: shinychat's new
getting-started API, which gives you a polished chat UI with all of
these niceties out of the box, and the lower-level plumbing beneath it
(ellmer and chatlas) that handles the connection to the LLM. We'll also
see how these building blocks power domain-specific applications like
querychat, and why they're designed to be general enough for essentially
any LLM-powered Shiny app. Examples in R, with Python equivalents
available for everything we'll cover.

title: AI Agents for Data Science: Posit Assistant, Commons, and Beyond
abstract:
Last year at posit::conf, we at Posit unveiled two new data science
agents: Positron Assistant and Databot. Your feedback was loud and
clear: having two Posit agents was confusing. So this year we’re back
with three new Posit agents!

In all seriousness, last year’s two agents merged their strengths to
become Posit Assistant, which is now available in both Positron and
RStudio, on the desktop and in Posit Workbench, and supports lots of
different LLM providers and models. I’ll explain why we think the design
choices we made in Posit Assistant make it the best agent for both data
work and for coding.

I’ll give you an up close look at Commons, which lets you create
data-oriented AI agents for others in your organization to use, and
includes our latest ideas for making data agents as trustworthy as
possible, even for non-experts.

And finally, I’ll give you a sneak peek at \[REDACTED\], our most
AI-forward data science tool yet.

title: AI Governance in Posit Team: getting trustworthy results from agentic helpers
abstract:
AI agents like Posit Assistant, pi, Claude Code, and Codex are here to
stay. Ensuring the results you deliver are trustworthy when agents do
some of the work can be daunting. In this talk, we’ll explore how
Governance done well is not bureaucracy but is empowering for the
individual as well as the organization, offer some useful definitions of
Risk and Compliance, and take a tour through emerging governance
capabilities including open source desktop agentic tools, Posit.AI Pass
Zero Data Retention access to curated models, and upcoming Posit Team
features for putting supervision and guardrails around your agents.

title: VIRTUAL WORKSHOP: Getting Started with Positron: An AI-Ready Polyglot Workflow for Data Science
abstract:
This virtual three hour workshop provides a quick start for R and Python
users who are curious about Positron, Posit’s new AI-ready polyglot code
editor for data science. Here, you will learn how to use Positron’s time
saving features to do a typical end-to-end data science task. Along the
way, you will learn how to:

- Install packages and set up a reproducible environment
- Connect to a database
- Add Positron Extensions 
- Navigate the Command Palette
- Configure Positron to use your favorite LLM model provider
- Write, Edit, and Debug code with Positron’s built in AI Client
- Use an LLM to explain and translate code
- Learn the best practices for cleaning and exploring data with LLMs
- Publish APIs, docs, apps and more with the Posit Publisher extension

This workshop will be a good fit for you as long as you have a basic
familiarity with at least one of R or Python. No installation is
necessary. Posit will provide a cloud environment equipped with both
Positron and the LLMs we will use during class.

title: Administering and Orchestrating Next-Gen Statistical Environments for AI and Open Source Enabled Infrastructure for Regulated Use Cases
abstract:
This workshop will explore practical approaches to building
reproducible, well-governed R environments for regulated pharmaceutical
work. We will discuss package management, risk-based package validation,
deployment options such as containers and managed platforms, and the
controls needed to support traceability, change management, and
production readiness. Through interactive discussion, participants will
consider what a minimum viable approach looks like for administering R
environments across research, development, and GxP use cases. We’ll also
look at the impact of AI on regulated environments.

title: AI-Powered Clinical Reporting in R with the Pharmaverse
abstract:
Modern clinical reporting workflows are evolving fast, and this workshop
helps you keep pace with a practical, end-to-end approach in R. You’ll
learn how to move from raw data to analysis deliverables using
Pharmaverse tools, including standards-aligned SDTM preparation,
efficient creation of ADaM datasets, and generation of high-quality
tables, listings, and graphs (TLGs) supported by Analysis Results
Datasets (ARDs). You’ll also see where AI-assisted tooling can fit
naturally into the workflow to support faster iteration and reduce
manual rework, without sacrificing transparency, reproducibility, or
reviewability. Leave with a modular, reusable playbook for applying R to
every stage of clinical reporting across your team.

title: Modern Data Science in Python
abstract:
As the data science landscape evolves, many practitioners are looking to
expand their toolkit to include Python. Led by Jeroen Janssens, author
of the book *Python Polars: The Definitive Guide* and Rich Iannone,
creator of the Great Tables package, this workshop will provide a
practical, hands-on introduction to an end-to-end Python workflow.

We will move beyond the basics of syntax to focus on a modern stack that
prioritizes readability and performance. Using Positron as our
development environment, we’ll navigate a complete project lifecycle.
The workshop covers:

- Data Manipulation: performant data wrangling using Polars.
- Visualization: implementing the Grammar of Graphics in Python with
  Plotnine.
- Reporting: creating presentation-ready tables with Great Tables.
- Modeling: building machine learning models using Scikit-Learn.

The workshop is structured around a single case study. You’ll work
through a series of exercises designed to help you get familiar with
these tools. By the end of the day, you’ll have a good idea of how to
translate your data science skills into a Python context and a
repository of code examples to apply to future projects. 

This workshop is a great fit for those getting started with data science
as well as R users who want to get their feet wet with Python for doing
data science.

title: Our Modern R Workflow (ft. Positron and AI)
abstract:
This workshop is designed for data scientists who are comfortable with
using R for data analysis and ready to level up their software
engineering skills. Led by Hadley Wickham and Jenny Bryan, you’ll learn
how to write more robust, maintainable R code while taking advantage of
modern tooling (cough AI cough) that can dramatically accelerate your
productivity.

We’ll cover three interconnected themes. First, you’ll learn
contemporary R development practices—writing functions, organizing code
into packages, testing, and documentation strategies that scale from
personal projects to team collaboration. Second, we’ll explore how AI
assistants like Claude Code can help you write better R code faster.
Third, we’ll share practical tips for getting the most out of Positron,
including features specifically designed to make R development and data
exploration more fluid.

Throughout the workshop, we’ll emphasize the connections between these
topics: how good development practices make AI assistance more
effective, how modern tooling reduces friction so you can focus on the
interesting problems, and how to build workflows that are both efficient
and reproducible. You’ll leave with concrete skills you can apply
immediately to your own projects.

Prerequisites: Basic familiarity with R programming (e.g. using the
tidyverse). You should have written a few functions before, but don’t
need any experience with package development, AI coding tools, or
Positron. If you have taken a package development workshop before,
you’ll learn what’s changed in our workflows, especially how we’re using
AI and Positron effectively.

title: Practical Machine Learning with tidymodels
abstract:
Learn how to successfully develop Machine Learning using R. tidymodels
is a complete framework that implements modeling best practices using
tidyverse principles. The tidymodels framework is a collection of
packages for modeling and machine learning using tidyverse principles. 

Led by Max Kuhn and Emil Hvitfeldt, this workshop will teach you core
tidymodels packages to preprocess data, specify and train models, and
optimize the tuning parameter. You’ll learn tidymodels syntax as well as
the process of predictive modeling for tabular data. Time permitting,
you’ll be introduced to basic pre-processing with recipes.

This workshop is for you if you:

- Are comfortable using tidyverse packages to read data into R,
  transform and reshape data, and make a variety of graphs, and
- Have some experience with modeling, such as linear regression,
  logistic regression, or tree-based models. 

While the workshop will teach some terminology and modeling philosophy,
it is primarily focused on showing users how to effectively develop,
iterate, and validate a machine learning model.

title: Practical Quarto: Patterns, Templates, and Tooling
abstract:
This workshop is designed for Quarto users who want to update and extend
their Quarto mastery. Led by Charlotte Wickham and Mine
Çetinkaya-Rundel, this workshop will introduce new features of Quarto as
well as blend practical recipes with conceptual understanding, so you
can both copy–paste what works and understand why it works. Rather than
a linear tour of Quarto features, the workshop is organized as a
collection of focused, reusable patterns—each one solving a real
authoring or publishing problem you’re likely to encounter.

Themes will include:

- Design once, use anywhere: Learn how to work effectively with light
  and dark modes, brands, and renderings, and how to share a consistent
  brand across multiple Quarto projects without duplication or
  fragility.
- Build reusable structures: Use template partials to factor out
  repeated content and layouts, making large or long-lived projects
  easier to maintain and evolve.
- Understand why Typst matters: Explore why Typst deserves a place on
  your radar, with concrete “quick wins” that show how it can
  dramatically simplify PDF generation.
- Work productively in Positron: Pick up Positron- and Quarto-specific
  productivity tips, including auto-formatting with Air, and practical
  ways to incorporate LLMs into your Quarto workflow.
- Master freezing and reproducibility: Demystify freeze—when to check it
  in to version control, when to refresh it, and how to use it
  intentionally to balance reproducibility, performance, and
  collaboration.

By the end of the workshop, you’ll have a curated set of Quarto recipes
and a mental model for how the pieces fit together. You’ll leave the
workshop equipped to create more polished documents, scale your
workflows across projects and teams, and make deliberate, informed
choices about tools, formats, and authoring strategies.

title: Programming with LLMs in R and Python
abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) offer developers unprecedented programmatic
capabilities. Led by Garrick Aden-Buie and Sara Altman, this workshop
will introduce ellmer (R) and chatlas (Python), Posit packages that
simplify LLM API integration, handling conversation complexities and
enabling seamless interactions with AI models. You’ll gain a conceptual
understanding of both ecosystems, but you can choose your own adventure
(R or Python) for hands-on coding sessions. 

Participants will explore system prompt design, token management, and
tool calling while building familiarity with current AI technologies.
The workshop demonstrates that:

- Coding with LLMs unlocks possibilities beyond standard tools
- No advanced AI background is required
- Implementing AI can be both accessible and exciting

Designed for AI newcomers and experienced developers, the session covers
LLM integration, Shiny web app development, and touches on advanced
topics like dynamic information retrieval, context engineering, and
agentic workflows. Attendees will gain hands-on experience through
guided exercises, providing the confidence to start their LLM journey.
As a dual-language workshop, attendees can choose hands-on practice in R
or Python.

- Learn the best practices for cleaning and exploring data with LLMs
- Publish APIs, docs, apps and more with the Posit Publisher extension

This workshop will be a good fit for you as long as you have a basic
familiarity with at least one of R or Python. No installation is
necessary. Posit will provide a cloud environment equipped with both
Positron and the LLMs we will use during class.

title: Welcome Reception
Virtual Session: Modeling
abstract:
This virtual session will have 4 20-minute talks!

- **AI/ML SOS IDK \| Olivia Hebner and Kathryn Cronquist \| Summit**\
  Many data scientists working in R are comfortable with regression but
  feel overwhelmed when getting started with machine learning. Often the
  challenge isn’t the algorithms, it’s knowing how to structure a clean,
  reproducible workflow. In this session, we’ll provide a
  beginner-friendly on-ramp to machine learning using tidymodels within
  Posit tools. Through a simple random forest example, we’ll demonstrate
  how data splitting, preprocessing, model specification, and evaluation
  fit together. Attendees will leave with a clear starting framework
  they can immediately apply to their own ML projects in R.
- **Nowcasting Pertussis Case Counts in Washington State \| Allie Warren
  \| Washington State Department of Health**\
  Pertussis is a highly contagious respiratory infection, but pertussis
  surveillance can lag by weeks due to delays between symptom onset and
  reporting and the need for case investigations, limiting timely
  outbreak response. Nowcasting—forecasting the present from incomplete
  data—addresses this gap by estimating the final case count for a given
  onset date. At the Washington State Department of Health, we
  implemented a process to track the pertussis reporting delays and used
  the epinowcast R package to model current pertussis case counts.
  Nowcasting reduced the timeframe from 9 weeks for complete data to 2
  weeks for reliable estimates, improving real-time awareness of
  pertussis trends, which allows for earlier interventions during
  outbreaks.
- **Beyond Prediction: A Causal Framework using R for solving real world
  problems \| Kimberley Isabel Orozco Cornejo \| ixpantia**\
  Standard machine learning excels at prediction, but often fails to
  answer strategic questions like: "What caused this?" or "What if we
  intervened?". Stakeholders need causal answers, not just correlations.
  In "Beyond Prediction, A Causal Framework using R for solving real
  world problems" we'll tackle a churn scenario where predictive models
  give wrong advice due to Simpson's Paradox. I will demonstrate how to
  build a reproducible causal framework in R. Using dagitty to map
  assumptions and other R packages to orchestrate data simulation,
  attendees will learn to build an in silico laboratory. People will
  leave knowing how to disentangle true effects from spurious
  correlations to drive reliable decision-making using R.
- **Interpretable NLP for Clinical Imaging: Using tidymodels and
  Lasso-Regularized Text Models to Classify Pleural Effusion Impressions
  in R \| Kaitlyn Housel \| University of Pennsylvania**\
  Clinical imaging reports contain critical diagnostic information, but
  their free-text format limits large-scale analysis. This talk presents
  an interpretable NLP pipeline built in R using tidymodels and
  lasso-regularized logistic regression to classify radiology
  impressions for pleural effusion. To improve clinical usefulness, I
  developed complementary functions that extract structured signals for
  effusion size and loculations, reducing ambiguity and strengthening
  model performance. The workflow emphasizes reproducibility and
  auditability, combining sparse text features with domain feature
  engineering. Attendees will learn a practical approach for modeling
  clinical text and strategies for augmenting statistical models with
  rule-based logic.

title: Virtual Session: Practical Workflows
abstract:
There are 3 20-minute talks in this session!

- **Let Your LLM Surprise You: Inbox Insights with ellmer and Posit
  Connect \| Konstantinos Ntentes \| Posit**\
  What if your team received a fresh, data-backed marketing insight
  every morning—without anyone writing it? In this talk, I’ll walk
  through how ellmer connects our enterprise LLM to sales-and-marketing
  funnel views, and how Posit Connect and blastula turn that output into
  actionable, inbox-ready insights with a supporting gt table and
  reproducible code chunk. I’ll also share how we balance analysis
  guardrails with creative freedom, maintain variety across runs, why
  misses are still useful, and how this work fits into our team’s
  roadmap toward trustworthy natural-language access to complex
  analytics for non-coder stakeholders.
- **An R app for generating appraisals reports \| Michael Morales \|
  INTUS**\
  Where I work, one of the teams used to write property appraisal
  reports in a spreadsheet. Each one had to do the edition, formatting,
  calculations, pictures, in a file saved locally in their computers.\
  We wanted to design an app that helped them to create the report, to
  just enter the parameters and pictures, and let the program do the
  formatting, the calculations, download the report, and saving the
  information into the cloud facilitating the data extraction.\
  And this is how we came out with PAO, which can be translated as
  Platform for appraisals Online, an app written in R via shinyapps,
  that uses officeR, flextable, bslib, etc, connects to AWS’ S3 and RDS,
  to save pictures and data into databases, facilitating their daily
  work.
- **Positron Notebooks: Built Around How You Actually Work \| Nick
  Strayer \| Posit**\
  At this conference you will find no shortage of presentations on what
  Positron does, but I want to focus on the why of the Positron Notebook
  Editor. We talked to data scientists across a variety of data science
  teams about how they work in notebooks day to day. Those conversations
  shaped how we built the Positron Notebook Editor.\
  The goal is the feeling you loved in RStudio, where everything you
  need is right at your fingertips, extended into notebooks: the
  features you need where they feel natural. IDE features like the
  interactive data explorer and kernel-aware AI assistant live right
  inside your notebook workflow. We'll demo the full loop live:
  exploring data, visualizing it, and sharing results out to
  stakeholders.

title: Virtual Session: Quarto, R + Python
abstract:
This virtual session will have 4 20-minute talks!

- **I Didn't Abandon R—I Added Python: My Story of Growing Without
  Starting Over \| Bilikisu Wunmi Olatunji \| R-Ladies Global/ R-Ladies
  Abuja**\
  I built my consulting career with R. It helped me deliver analyses,
  dashboards, reports, and models that clients trusted. Then I started
  seeing opportunities that were a perfect fit for my experience—but
  they expected Python. Like many people, I told myself I wasn't ready.\
  This talk is the story of how I stopped letting a programming language
  define my professional identity and started building on what I already
  knew. Through a real consulting project—not a code walkthrough—I’ll
  share the practical playbook that helped me transition confidently:
  Wrap → Validate → Swap. Along the way, I'll show how lightweight
  metric contracts and golden datasets helped me keep results consistent
  while working across R and Python.\
  You'll leave with practical ideas for expanding your opportunities,
  navigating mixed-language environments with confidence, and growing
  your career without feeling like you have to start over.
- **Combining Agentic Python Applications with R Workflows Using Posit
  Connect \| Luis Wirth \| HMS Analytical Software**\
  Companies rely on R for their analytical workflows, while Python now
  supports agentic LLM-based systems, motivating architectures that
  combine both ecosystems.\
  This talk presents a system where a Python application acts as a
  frontend and an agentic orchestrator and delegates code execution to
  an R backend. Both applications are deployed on Posit Connect via an
  automatic git deployment workflow. The apps communicate via API calls,
  allowing the agent to trigger R-based tasks such as data wrangling,
  plotting, and statistical calculations. Using a real system with demo
  data, we focus on presenting architecture and deployment patterns and
  discuss benefits and tradeoffs compared to all-Python or all-R
  designs.
- **Shift-left for more accessibility \| Björn Fisseler \|
  FernUniversität in Hagen**\
  Quarto lets authors produce reports, slides, and dashboards from
  plain-text source files, but these outputs aren’t accessible by
  default. This talk presents practical workflows, tools, and design
  guidelines to build accessible Quarto content from the start. I cover
  the POUR principles, semantic document structure, accessible tables
  and figures, alt-text strategies for plots, and comparisons of R
  packages and AI-assisted approaches for generating descriptions.
  Attendees will leave with a checklist, examples, and methods for
  manual and automated accessibility testing to integrate into
  reproducible workflows.
- **Where Do Notebooks Come From? \| Wasim Lorgat \| Posit**\
  Quarto and Jupyter are two of the most widely used tools in
  computational notebooks, but they offer very different experiences.
  Why is that?\
  This talk traces two threads of development that led to where we are
  today, from Donald Knuth's vision of writing code as narrative, a
  tradition that eventually led to Quarto, as well as John McCarthy's
  interactive LISP paradigm whose legacy inspired the scientific Python
  tools that led to Jupyter.\
  These threads are now converging, with the Positron IDE at the
  intersection, bringing the literate program and the interactive
  notebook together in one environment.\
  I hope this talk gives you a new way to think about the tools you use
  every day, and the confidence to try the ones you don't.

title: Do This Instead: 4 Alternatives to Common Charts
abstract:
Even in “good” charts, it’s easy to miss or misinterpret key patterns in
the data. Common best practices — continuous color scales, equally
spaced gridlines, month-level aggregation, etc — leave critical leaps
from numbers to meaning up to visual perception and unexamined
assumptions. “Do This Instead” offers 5 specific before/after
replacements for common analysis situations. For example, grouping
continuous values into meaningful categories lets us use facet_wrap to
create small multiples instead of relying on color perception. And,
explicitly defining what counts as “high” creates a shared,
expertise-grounded interpretation. Techniques are tool-agnostic;
examples implemented in ggplot.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

title: Quack to the Future: Building Traceable Data Lakehouses with DuckLake in R
abstract:
Modern data pipelines need more than clean outputs: they need a paper
trail. This talk introduces two R packages to help you build a lakehouse
stack using DuckLake for transactional storage and dplyneage for
column-level lineage tracking. We'll walk through a medallion
architecture (bronze → silver → gold) built with dplyr familiar
workflows, where every table write is versioned with author and commit
message. You'll see how to visualize lineage flows across pipeline
layers, time-travel back to earlier table versions, and audit exactly
how your data changed and why, all without leaving R.

title: Building a Custom Version of GeoGuessr in R
abstract:
This is about using R creatively for non-traditional tasks, with an
example of building a custom version of the game GeoGuessr in R.
Attendees at this session will learn not only about the tools to build
this, but how to innovatively solve problems in R. The process starts by
taking a non-technical idea: a version of GeoGuessr just for New York
City. Then breaking it down into smaller parts that R can handle:
developing a Shiny dashboard frontend for players to interact with,
encoding gameplay into data structures in Google Sheets for easy access
for players, and building a backend to collect and process data from
APIs. Attendees can play the live game with locations from the host
city, Houston, to see R powering real-time gameplay.

title: ORCA: a collaboratively-built AI-powered Shiny app built on Posit Team
abstract:
ORCA is KS&R’s internal Shiny application for AI-assisted coding of
open-ended survey responses. Designed in concert with Ketchbrook
Analytics, ORCA combines an intuitive front-end for job submission,
response review, and code editing with a modular backend built on the
Posit ecosystem. The system integrates a {golem}-based Shiny app, a
plumber API for asynchronous processing, pins for versioned metadata,
and scheduled batch workflows for logging and delivery. This talk
showcases how thoughtful UI/UX design and Posit-based infrastructure
work together to operationalize AI in a transparent, reproducible
research environment.

title: Reusing 'ggplot2' code: how to design better plot helper functions
abstract:
Creating 'ggplot2' helper functions can help avoid repeatedly copying
and pasting long and complex 'ggplot2' code chunks. However, if helper
functions are not carefully designed, the initial convenience can often
turn into frustration. While helper functions can reduce the amount of
code needed to remake a complicated plot, they often mask the underlying
layered grammar of graphics, complicating further customisation and
tweaking of the plot. This talk addresses how to design effective
'ggplot2' plot helper functions that maximise reuse convenience whilst
preserving access to the elegant flexibility of layered plot
composition.

title: From Dplyr to Polars: Migrating Tools & Languages While Maintaining the Tidy Model
abstract:
Many data practitioners who learned analysis through R’s dplyr, discover
that moving to Python can feel like losing a native language. I
certainly felt that way, and my colleagues tend to echo the same
sentiments. Learning new syntax is easy, but porting the mental model
the tidyverse provides was the real challenge. In this talk I describe
my personal migration from dplyr to Polars and how I rebuilt the mental
model in a new ecosystem. I draw on my personal opinions and experience,
the thoughts of colleagues, and the objective differences in technical
goals and specifications. The goal of this talk is to show data
practitioners how to preserve the workflows they loved in dplyr with the
execution model of polars in python.

title: From internal scripts to public portfolios: building an open source program at Dow
abstract:
Dow's Citizen Data Science community is putting R and Python into the
hands of chemical researchers across the company. As these data science
workflows matured, we saw an opportunity: share our general-purpose
tools with the broader community through an open source release program.
This talk walks through how we built that program -- the policy, the
legal review process, the release checklist -- and piloted it with six R
packages for statistical analysis and experimental design. Attendees
will leave with a practical playbook for standing up an open source
release program at organizations where one doesn't yet exist.

title: Life after R4DS: How to take your R skills to the next level
abstract:
Picture this: You've taken that difficult first step into learning R,
and you've worked your way through a course, workshop, or online
textbook like "R for Data Science". Your foundation is solid - but now
what?\
\
This talk will give you the resources you need to take your R skills to
the next level. First, I will discuss the three ABCs of pathways forward
to Intermediate R: Analysis of complex data, Building professional
deliverables, and Coding/programming.\
\
Then, I will share a new public course site designed for both classroom
use and for self-guided learners. The course takes a "learn by doing"
approach, with modular tracks structured around project that is
completed progressively through hands-on exercises.

title: Cairn: From notebooks to logbooks
abstract:
Notebooks let you rewrite history. Logbooks don't. In logbook-mode
analysis, history is a first-class citizen: cells, commentary, and AI
exchanges are only ever appended so that the document becomes a
chronological record of every step performed in a data analysis. I'll
show why notebook software doesn't fully accommodate this style, and
introduce Cairn, my attempt at supporting it properly: a Neovim plugin
for stacking your analysis one stone at a time.

title: Positron Everywhere All At Once
abstract:
A modern data science IDE has to feel the same wherever someone opens
it. Data scientists move constantly between personal laptops, shared
servers, containerized workflows, and the mix of cloud and on-prem
environments that shape day-to-day work. The tools they rely on need to
travel with them.

Positron, a next-generation data science IDE, is one of those tools.
Deploying it means meeting people on the platforms they already use. In
this talk, I'll share strategies for bringing Positron to academic
settings, where instructors and students juggle personal machines,
course JupyterHub deployments, and department servers. I'll walk through
real examples of running Positron Server through JupyterHub via
jupyter-server-proxy, configuring it for classroom use, and weighing the
tradeoffs of each approach. You'll leave with practical techniques for
common academic deployment scenarios and a clearer sense of where
Positron fits today.

title: From ABC to AI: Applying Language Acquisition to R and Technical Mastery
abstract:
The world’s most spoken language isn’t Python. It is English. As a
second language learner who struggled before later teaching English and
authoring a book on R, I learned that fluency comes from internalizing
structure. In the age of AI, if models can generate code instantly, does
learning R still matter? This talk introduces a Three Layer Model of
Technical Mastery: Syntax, the vocabulary that AI accelerates;
Structure, the grammar of tidyverse, Quarto, and Shiny workflows;
Thinking, the human skills of framing problems and making judgments. By
mapping language learning to the evolution of a data scientist, this
talk offers a practical framework for building durable skills in an AI
assisted world.

title: How Shiny changed data analysis at the Metabolism Center
abstract:
Scientists in metabolic research increasingly rely on technologies
measuring thousands of targets simultaneously, but many are still
limited to analyses in spreadsheets Introducing Shiny transformed how
our center works with data: an ecosystem of apps now gives researchers
tools that once required coding, enabling faster exploration and richer
insights. Data can be easily visualized with datasets from other
researchers, allowing analysis in a broader context. Junior researchers
are building new apps, sharing their analysis pipelines with the world.
I will share some of our success stories, and highlight the packages we
use to make apps fast, interactive, and intuitive.

title: Quarto Hub: Collaboratively edit, create, and share documents
abstract:
Quarto Hub is a new open-source and hosted platform from Posit. In
Quarto Hub, you can create, edit, comment on, and publish your Quarto
projects (single documents, presentations, websites) collaboratively. In
this talk, we will give an overview of how it works, and how Quarto Hub
interacts with existing code-first practices and text-based workflows.
We will show how the architecture of Quarto Hub allows a variety of use
cases, including (if time permits) integration with RStudio, Positron,
and Posit AI.

title: From, "Can you Just Make Us a Dashboard" to Enterprise Systems in R
abstract:
Over the past five years, Mayo Clinic’s Data Visualization Lab has grown
from three statisticians building simple dashboards in R into an
enterprise team delivering production Shiny systems that support real
clinical and operational decision-making. This talk shares lessons
learned from scaling open-source tools in a highly regulated healthcare
environment, where data are siloed, workflows are complex, and trust
matters. I’ll discuss how we moved from ad-hoc dashboards to governed,
maintainable applications using R, Shiny, REDCap, and Posit Connect, and
what it took organizationally to make the shift succeed. Attendees will
leave with concrete patterns for building credibility and responsibly
scaling R-based systems in high-stakes settings.

title: Instant Feedback, Robust Evals: Agentic AI Tutoring in R and Python
abstract:
What if every open source data science resource included practice coding
problems with immediate feedback? I made blendtutor and blendtutor-py so
educators can hand-craft coding lessons installed as an R package or
Python module. Learners then get immediate agentic AI-powered feedback
on their code. And we don’t have to just hope the LLMs provide useful
pointers. These packages give scaffolding to create custom LLM evals for
every lesson. No matter the learning goal, educators can create lessons
where LLMs steer learners in a helpful direction. The best version of
these packages involves co-evolution with the community. I’m excited to
figure out together how this active learning can support other open
source resources.
